64:## (b) Consequential, by theme
66:### The checker's typing and inference (9)
68:2. **The checker's third and fourth attempts at a call.** His decision on the order of the checker's attempts at a call names two: by subtyping without the expected type first, then by coercion with it. Batch 8's rung I kept a third between them, by subtyping with the expected type, so that a call whose untyped function argument only the expected type can fix still type-checks. It also kept a fourth, last: coercion without the expected type (`compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/decision-record.md:57`, D4, the built order; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:733-737`). P-49 states the two attempts of his decision, and F-78 gives all four in order and says which two an agent chose. No source says whether his review of this item covers the fourth; a cold reader of P-49 took the fourth as approved, since only the third is marked.
75:3. **A declaration chosen statically keeps its inferred instance.** Batch 7b's rung S wrote that a declaration the static call selected keeps the instance inferred for it. Where neither the call's static return type nor an invariant position constrains a type parameter, this departs from the POPL 2019 paper, whose rule his decision on the instance follows.
82:4. **Does the inference chapter solve a call's type parameters together?** For `loneT[\S, T extends S\](a: T, b: T, s: S)` over an Apple, a Pear and a Pear, walk gives both parameters `Fruit`. Read one parameter at a time, the chapter gives `S` the type of `s` alone, and then `T` has no instance.
89:5. **Do `try`, `catch` and `atomic` bodies take the expected type?** He ruled that a `typecase` clause and a `label` body take the expected type of the whole. A `try` and an `atomic` have the same shape in the text: the type of a `try` is the union of its block's and its `catch` clauses' types, and an `atomic` has its body's type.
96:175. **Where a conditional extension's condition holds: the other `extends` entries.** A trait or object may extend a type under a `where` clause, as `object Bad[\E\](x: E) extends { Wrap[\E\], Shows where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }` does. Climb batch 18's rung X first checked the whole `extends` clause under every condition, so it accepted that declaration, which the base refuses and whose run died at link time. Its skeptic's contested fix `bd18b6a47` checks each entry with its own conditions, and the members with all of them. The judge upheld the fix.
103:176. **Where a conditional extension's condition holds: the header.** After rung X, the checker still checked a declaration's static parameters, its own `where` clause, its `throws` clause and contract, and its `excludes` and `comprises` clauses with every conditional entry's condition holding. So it accepted three programs that the base refuses, 'Ill-formed type: W[\E\] ... does not satisfy the corresponding bound Shows.': an `excludes` entry, a `comprises` entry and a static parameter's bound, each well formed only under the condition. Rung X's judge saw it by reading (X.judge.2), and the merged-diff review ran it (review.1).
110:177. **Where an object's value parameters fall under a conditional extension.** Nothing on record settles it. A value parameter that is not transient is a field (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:271-272`), and P-151 puts the members under the condition. The constructor's arrow type holds at every instance (`objects.tex:204-206`).
117:178. **The members of a conditional extension scoped to the condition (row 773).** The checker checks a member under a conditional extension's condition, as P-151 says. The member stays callable where the condition fails, since the members a type inherits are read at every instance: `Lst[\Fn\](Fn(inc), Fn(inc)).lt(...)` compiles, and its run dies at link time, 'NoSuchMethodError: ... CondExtendMember$Fn.lt(CondExtendMember$Fn)'. Swift, Rust and Haskell scope such members to the condition. The scoping waited on row 748's check at a dotted call, which rung K landed in the same batch; that check reads a method's own `where` clause only, so row 773 holds.
124:212. **How far a self-typed trait reaches: the team's `Containment` mixins (P-146).** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. P-146's text refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type. The team's 2009 mixins `ContainmentBySubset[\T extends Containment[\T\]\] extends Containment[\T\]` and `ContainmentByComparison` extend `Containment` at their parameter `T`, not at themselves, so the text refuses them. Yet their `T` is the implementing type: `Relation[\T\]` extends `ContainmentBySubset[\Relation[\T\]\]`. The questions that he answered with "1." on 2026-10-13 (23:06 UTC and after) defined a self-typed trait as "a generic trait whose parameter stands for the type that implements it", with `Integral` as the example; the entry's wording is the self-typed bodies judgement's. On 2026-10-13 at 23:59 UTC the coordinator put this to him as a separate choice. On 2026-10-14 at 00:07 UTC he did not recall wording anything about mixins, and said that he was far out of his depth. At 00:08 UTC the coordinator took the widening itself, on his review list, by the method that he approved at 00:12 UTC ("Yes, that's how I want it.").
131:### Overloading and the Meet Rule (8)
133:6. **The Meet Rule's closed-trait case for generic families.** Item 26 gave the Meet Rule a case for two closed traits: declarations over the listed types cover their intersection. The text applies it to declarations with static parameters too; the checker refuses it there. Since batch 8, the functional-method form is accepted and dies at run time (row 566); the function form is still refused.
140:7. **An identical coercion on every candidate.** `choose(S, ZZ64)`, `choose(T, ZZ64)` and `choose(V, ZZ64)` called with a `ZZ32` need the same coercion for every candidate. Does that count as the conversion being fixed, so that the call is typed by the intersection of the return types?
147:8. **Coverage of functional methods below the providing type.** A functional method is a method called as a function, `f(x)`, with `self` among its parameters. The checker judges coverage in each type that provides the two methods, over what that type provides. A trait between the two closed traits that provides both and declares nothing (`SkFnBetween`) is refused compiled and runs under walk.
154:9. **Exclusion through a bound, and `tint` (row 786).** Do two parameter types exclude each other when the only static arguments at which they could meet are ones a bound rules out? Walk loads `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, reading two type parameters whose bounds exclude as never one type, and the checker refuses the pair; `Bottom` lies within both bounds and cannot be written, so which path moves is his.
161:10. **A written static argument on a name with a generic and a plain declaration.** For `op[\ZZ64\](z, w)`, where `op` has a generic and a plain declaration, walk runs the generic declaration's instance and the compiled run dispatches to the plain one. The text says nothing of a static argument written on such a name.
168:11. **A family that mixes a function with functional methods.** Over two closed traits, a family that mixes a top-level function with functional methods is refused on both paths. The chapter's rule for functions and its rule for functional methods both apply to it, and neither says which governs.
175:13. **The approved `comprises` check decides by names.** The 14 lines of the checker's `comprises` check that he approved decide by how a type that extends the trait spells its type variable, and by simple names: an unrelated trait of the same name counts, and a false clause can pass.
182:228. **Is the type group's paper of 2011 the reason for P-152?** P-152 has walk and the checker read exclusion between two generic declarations over the whole parameter type. On 2026-10-17 at 11:36 UTC he chose it: "Agreed. Only one option makes sense. The option one." He gave no reason. The question put to him gave the specification's text as the reason. The review that he ordered on 2026-10-19 at 21:38 UTC, of every design decision taken on the recommendation of the cheaper Haiku model, found that this text is the revival's own (`576b4c287`), which restates the type group's paper of 2011. So `ba93d28ec` replaced the reason with the paper. A Fable judge found that the decision stands (`coordinator/postmortem-2026-10-19-haiku/fable-judgement.md:23`). No message of his reviews the new reason.
189:### Walk's checks at load (2)
191:15. **Which `comprises` clauses walk checks at load.** Since batch 9, walk checks `comprises` clauses when it loads a program, but only the main component's. The text and the checker read every clause.
198:232. **After the switch-over, does walk refuse a program that the checker refuses (P-12)?** P-12 says that after the switch-over walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, gains their static types, and then uses the coercions that the checker inserts. Its reason: "The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs." On 2026-09-15 at 10:42 UTC he asked to run the type checker "optionally" in walk. No message of his says which of two things he wants: a checker that walk runs only when asked, or a walk that refuses every program that the checker refuses.
205:### Walk's choice of declaration and instance (3)
207:18. **Walk's choice when another declaration applies without coercion.** `g(a: Any, b: Any)` beside `g[\T\](a: T, b: T)`, called with an Apple and a Cherry, which share more than one closest supertype: walk ran the plain declaration, as the base did. Since climb batch 17's rung G, walk refuses this unbounded pair at load by the No Duplicates Rule; the choice stays for the pair with `T extends Fruit`, which row 589's test `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXDispatchTwoCommonParentsWalk.fss` now writes.
214:19. **The open type wins at dispatch.** Since batch 11, walk leaves open a parameter whose bound names itself, when nothing fixes it. A declaration whose parameter has the open type is then the most specific: in a `Holder[\OPEN\]`, `take(x: T)` runs for 3 where `take(x: ZZ32)` ran, and accepts a string it used to refuse. For tuples (row 663) it goes the other way: `pick(x: Any)` wins over `pick(x: (T,T))`.
221:210. **Walk fixes an unwritten reduction's type parameter by its elements.** A reduction, such as `SUM[j <- 0#3] j`, or a comprehension may leave its big operator's static argument unwritten. At such a call, climb batch 15's rung B has walk fix the parameter by the declared type of the expression's value, else by the join of its elements' run-time types, else at the bound, in place of `Bottom` (ways 6 and 7 of the walk probe, `perf-probes/walk-plain-bound/REPORT.md`, section 1). It is the coordinator's first call in climb batch 15's record. The call reads P-48's "never ... the value's type alone" as not reaching a parameter that the desugaring fixes by the expression's type, for which walk's elements stand in, and P-59, walk's choice of coercions by the value, as covering this choice too. The record says so itself: "Call 1 reads past the letter of one, P-48's last clause" (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-15.md`, section 2). The clarity pass of 2026-10-22 kept that clause in P-48 and added: "Under walk, dispatch takes the value's type, and always will, since walk has no static types." A cold reader of the new text read the two as a contradiction unless the clause holds only on the compiled path; that reading bears on this item's question. He has not seen it. Item 17 (unwritten reductions whose parameter has a plain bound) was settled by the coordinator under P-48 on 2026-10-14, after his message of 07:10 UTC, in which he did not recall the question.
228:### Numbers and numerals (14)
230:20. **`widen` of a `ZZ` too large for `ZZ64` (item 31).** `widen` turns an unbounded integer into a 64-bit one. No passage says what it does when the value does not fit.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## The specification and the repository's lineage

FACTS.md:223
- F-171 **The specification reads a `comprises` clause as the restart's Types chapter does: every value of the trait is a value of a listed type.** So a trait or object that extends the closed trait must be below a listed type, with two exceptions. A trait with a `comprises` clause of its own may stay unlisted if each of its own listed types is below a listed type of the closed trait. A trait with static parameters may stay unlisted if at least one type extends it and every type that extends it is below a listed type. A listed type may be an instantiation at the trait's static parameters or `where`-clause variables. The text does not say whether a bare type variable may be listed; walk overflows its stack on one (row 407). The compiled checker departs in three ways: it checks only the closed trait's immediate subtypes (row 487), it reads the clause in the subtrait's own type-variable names (row 489), and it finds extenders by the simple text of a name (row 490). Whether the team's commented `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]` is valid is open (F-121). FACTS.md:91
- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, save in the overloading check's exclusion test (F-277), and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` is instead the trait met with the union of those types, and the exclusion test reads its signatures plain. **
 * The type %Contains[\T\]% "contains" objects of type %T%, in the sense
 * that we can check whether a %T% is a member of a %Contains[\T\]% using
 * %opr IN% and its ken, or using a %case% expression. *)
trait Contains[\T\]
    (** %opr IN% indicates whether %self% contains %elt% **)
    abstract opr IN(elt:T, self): Boolean
    (** The %MATCH% operator is used (as a temporary hack) by case when the
        match clause is a %Contains[\T\]%.  We must choose either %=%, %SEQV%, or
        %IN% as appropriate, depending on the type of the LHS. **)
    opr MATCH(x:Any, self): Boolean
end

content.content:
- the arrays exclude `{ Number, String }` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2215`, `:2411`, `:2785`).

The api writes the clause for `Rank` and the arrays but none for `Range` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2095`): the team placed `Range`'s exclusion in the component only.

**The crash's site.** Four precedents:
- the team's stopgap: "It should use a parameterized Generator type but it is not yet supported. Instead, we use GeneratorZZ32 for now" (525264af1, 2009-10-02), with `Types.makeGeneratorType(NF.make_InferenceVarType(span))` left commented beside each use (now `Functionals.scala:874`);
- the checker already builds that parameterized form for a generator clause (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Misc.scala:103-106`);
- the world switch re-points four names between the two libraries, `STRING`, `JAVASTRING`, `EXCEPTION` and `CHECKED_EXCEPTION` (`Types.java:77-88`), and `WellKnownNames.areCompilerLibraries()` tells the worlds apart (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/WellKnownNames.java:141-143`);
- walk's own rule for a `case` without an operator asks whether the guard's value extends the generic trait `Contains` (`Evaluator.java:415`, `Glue.extendsGenericTrait(match.type(), WellKnownNames.containsTypeName)`).

**The same defect elsewhere.** The defect is a type the checker names that one world's library does not declare. Counted over `Types.java`'s makers and statics and their uses in `scala_src/`, there are two sites in the one-library direction, `GeneratorZZ32` and `Character`, and in the compiler world's direction `Region` and the five of the last bullet:
- *`UniformDistribution[\T\](range:FullScalarRange)` keeps its own parameter*, as the brief asks. Its body, `just range.lower` for a declared `Just[\T\]`, is now typed `ZZ32` against `T` for any `T` other than `ZZ32`; only `RandomTest` instantiates it, at `ZZ32`.
- *The tests' names:*
  - the refusal test `XXXRangeWideRungJ.fss`;
  - the guard test `RangeZZ32RungJ.fss`;
  - row 452's test renamed `RangeSizeRungO.fss`, keeping its provenance in the name and dropping the `XXX` and the width;
  - the compiled test `XXXRangeInRungJ.fss`, with `RangeInRungJLink.test` and `XXXRangeInRungJ.test`.

**The checker fix.** Files and lines: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/Types.java:133-139`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/impls/Functionals.scala:15` and `:866-883`.
- In the compiler's world the test is unchanged, `isSubtype(t, Types.makeGeneratorZZ32Type(span))`, with the commented parameterized form kept beside it.
- In the one-library world (`WellKnownNames.areCompilerLibraries()` false), the rule asks whether the guard's type and the condition's type, or one of their ancestors, is an instance of the generic trait `Contains`.
  - `Types.isContainsType` compares the trait's name with `fortressLibrary() + "." + containsTypeName`.
  - A type that is not a trait type answers false.
- The operator is then chosen as before: `IN` when the guard is a `Contains` and the condition is not, `=` otherwise.
- For a guard whose type is a trait type this is the specification's rule: "If the type of the guarding expression is a subtype of type `Contains` and the condition expression does not, the default operator is ∈; otherwise, it is =" (`Specification/basic/expressions/case.tex:47-51`). The one-library branch tests the guard's type only when it is a trait type, and that type's ancestors, and answers `=` for any other type.
  - For a guard typed by a type variable bounded by a `Contains`, or by a union of `Contains` types, it picks `=`. That differs from `case.tex:47-51`, which gives ∈; from walk, which tests the guard's value (`Evaluator.java:415`) and picks ∈; and, for the type variable, from the compiler's world, whose `isSubtype` reads the bound and picks ∈ (the skeptic's `probes/skeptic/sk-case-op-fix.txt`, `SkCaseGuards-walk.txt`, `sk-compile-op-C.txt`).
  - `=` applies to such a guard without error, so nothing reports it, and a compiled clause of that shape would never match. Row 480 holds it, homed in those probes as the crash is (section 10).
- The edit outside the `case` rule's lines is the import of `WellKnownNames` at `Functionals.scala:15` and the helper in `Types.java`.
- Ways not taken:
  - re-pointing `makeGeneratorZZ32Type` to `Generator[\ZZ32\]` in the one-library world: a `Generator` is not what the specification asks, and a `Contains` that is not a `Generator` would get `=`;
  - the team's parameterized form against an inference variable: `Generator` again, and the team's own note that it is not supported;
  - a static re-pointed by `useFortressLibraries()`: the one library has no non-generic counterpart of `GeneratorZZ32`, and `Contains[\T\]` needs its argument.
- `Types.CHARACTER` is not touched.

## 5. What the specification settles

- **The ranges' width: nothing.**
  - "Assume that a, b, and c are expressions that produce integer values" (`Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex:42-44`; read `:37-110`). The sets are at `:47`, `:54-56` and `:64-65`, and the size at `:103-106`.
  - The draft's own examples build `ZZ64` and `ZZ` ranges (FACTS.md, "The specification never wrote static-argument inference, a numeral's type hierarchy or a range's integer width").
  - The decision settles the width (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-27, the numerics plans, decision 1), and rung U writes it into the chapter.
- **Why generic range code cannot be checked.** "Types named by type parameters *do not have coercions*" (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex:363-365`; read `:267-387`), so a numeral never becomes an `I`. A `ZZ32` parameter takes a numeral through the library's coercion.
- **The `case` rule**: `Specification/basic/expressions/case.tex:47-51` (read `:25-75`), quoted above. The fix follows it in the one-library world for a guard whose type is a trait type. For a guard typed by a type variable bounded by a `Contains`, or by a union of `Contains` types, it answers `=` where the rule gives ∈, as walk (`Evaluator.java:415`, on the value) and, for the type variable, the compiler's world do not (section 4; `probes/skeptic/sk-case-op-fix.txt`, `SkCaseGuards-walk.txt`, `sk-compile-op-C.txt`; row 480).
- **`Range` and `String` excluding each other**: "If a trait T excludes a trait U, the two traits are mutually exclusive … the exclusion relation is symmetric" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:223-233`; read `:215-260`).
- **Whether a `String` operator may overload a generic range operator: not settled by the text as it stands.**
  - `Specification/basic/overloading.tex:100-107` makes it "an error for their static parameters to differ … or for one declaration to have static parameters and another to not have them". Every such set in the library breaks this, for example `opr #()` beside `opr #[\I\](r: PartialRange[\I\], size:I)`, on the base as after.
  - Answer 9 removes that sentence in favour of the type group's 2011 model, whose exclusion rules read each declaration's own bounds (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26, answer 9). The model is not yet written into the chapter.
- **`IN` on a range**: `ranges.tex:94`, with `:47` and `:64-65`: 4 is in `2:6`, and 6 is in `3#4`.

- P-26 **Where the type group's later positions conflict with the specification's early text, the later positions win.** The early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run, with performance as the goal and specialization a must, and learned what is feasible. Specialization, in the type group's design, is a special version of a generic function for one instantiation, such as `tail(x: List[ZZ])` beside `tail[X](x: List[X])`, which dispatch chooses at run time. Where the two conflict, the specification is revised to follow their later word (P-95 records each change with its reason). Their later word includes the exclusion rule, specialization kept, the number types of the compiler's prelude made siblings in 2009 and 2010 (P-43: the library's numbers are flat in the same way), Karl Naden's 2012 write-up "The Return Type Rule and Generics" (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex`) and the type group's POPL 2019 paper (F-166). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. The revival does not second-guess them: it knows less than they did.

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's distance stage: the compiled checker over the whole interpreter library, the
# twelve prelude apis and their twelve components, every stage of every unit run whatever
# the earlier stages reported, so that nothing hides behind an early return; one table.
#
# Why it exists: Pavol's answer 11 (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26): the full measurement of the
# distance to the switch-over "becomes a report-only stage of phase 3's gates, whose job is
# driving it down". The checker-count stage beside it (../checker-count/run.sh) sees only
# the errors before each api's early return, 62 of about 1,740 on 2026-09-27.
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched: the
# shadow sources and classes, the driver, the checker's caches (-Dfortress.caches) and the
# JVM's temporary directory (so Rats! leaves nothing in /tmp) go to the scratch directory
# (default: $TMPDIR or /tmp), and the caches are deleted at the end. It never removes
# /tmp/fortress*rats, which other runs on the machine use. Exit 0 if the table was
# produced, 1 if it could not be. One JVM, -Xmx4g, one busy core: 789 s on the idle 4-CPU
# container on 2026-09-27, 14 to 24 minutes under load 7 to 18 (switch-over-distance-flat.md
# section 5); the table's #seconds and #machine rows say what each run took and where.
#
# The setting: "any" by default, the compiled path with the implicit bound Any
# (DistanceMulti's -setting any: the extends-Object pre-desugaring off, as walk's, and the
# compiled-expression desugaring on, as the compile path's). Answer 11 names the compile
# path's setting; batch 7's question 1, answered (a) on 2026-09-27 (POSITIONS.md, the
# numerics plans), bounds an unbounded type parameter by Any, and under it the switch-over
# takes that bound for the compiled path (CLIMB-BATCH-7.md section 1, Q1), so the 372
# "bound Object" errors of the plain compile setting are the setting's, not the library's
# (switch-over-distance-flat.md sections 2.7 and 5: "under (a) the stage runs stage-any").
# On the tree of 2026-09-27 it differs from walk's setting by the compiled-expression
# desugaring's 12 abstract-method errors on bodyless functions, one export error and the
# variance checker's crash on Stream: 1,746 to 1,747 against 1,737 to 1,738 (FACTS.md,
# "The true distance to the switch-over"). The third argument, walk or compile, runs
# another setting, for a comparison with the measurements on file; the gate never passes it.
#
# The overloading checker's memo is off (-Dfortress.analyzer.overload.cache=false), as in
# every run of the measurement: keyed on declaration pairs, it hides 27 to 35 errors
# depending on the build order (FACTS.md, "The overloading checker's memo hides errors
# by build order, so every count runs with it off ...").
#
# The sources beside this script are copies, taken 2026-09-27, so that the gate does not
# depend on a probe directory, as the checker-count stage's were: DistanceMulti.java from
# perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat/ (35ef70584); shadow-patch.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen/ (e5d8cdbd2); add-patch.py and errors.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance/ (a7e3df9ad, 14d2f9839); classify.py from
# perf-probes/prelude/distance-triage/ (e17a9badc); all unchanged but classify.py, which since
# row 577 finds the library places that name three of its classes by their declarations in
# the tree's sources ($FH, passed to table.py), not by line ranges. table.py is new: it
# counts as those scripts count and prints the rows below. The shadow classes are not
# copies: they are made from the tracked sources at every run by text edits that must each
# match exactly once (shadow-patch.py, add-patch.py), so there is no copied checker to go
# stale silently; an edit that no longer matches stops the run before the checker starts,
# and the table then says so in its #shadow row, with no counts.
#
# The table, tab-separated, every row tagged:
#   #distance   the setting, the switches and the twelve targets
#   #total      distinct errors; or "none:" and why, when no total was measured, as when a
#               target stopped with errors the stage does not count, such as a parse error

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:35
- P-38 **The compiler prelude's defects are not repaired: they go with it at the switch-over.** Its `Maybe` block and its `REM` guard `if other = -1 then 0` stay as landed until the prelude is deleted, and their tests stay. Then the compiled tests respell its reversed wrapping and saturating operators (row 348), `ZZ64`'s compiled shift closes (row 381), and the specification's `shift` reaches the compiled path (row 383). `XXXShiftDeclRungI` is then promoted, and the switch-over batch finds the compiler tests that bind `shift`, a reserved name from then on.

POSITIONS.md:55
- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. Its string is to name a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, such as `"com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT"`, in place of a glue class of walk, which the compiled path cannot use (F-32). Walk is to load the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. At the parse, before the checker, the compiled path is to rewrite each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call, and to refuse a string that names no helper. The bindings move onto helpers step by step, and from the step that moves a binding, the compiled checker checks it against the helper's Java signature, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. The ground: the language has no foreign-function interface, which the Working Draft lists only among proposed features (`Specification/appendices/future.tex`). So the form of a binding belongs to Java interoperability (P-26 defines the layers), and the library's own practice decides it (P-27): every binding in the library is a `builtinPrimitive` call. The specification prints `builtinPrimitive` only inside the included library api, whose comment describes walk's mechanism; that is no ground. The choice is cheap to undo only until the bindings start to move onto helpers; after that, the other form costs a sweep of the library. Every binding still names a glue class. Row 796: walk loads a binding's string only as a glue class. Row 309: the compiled path has no counterpart of `builtinPrimitive`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## The goal

POSITIONS.md:12
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this, or for any other matter that needs the static types that the checker infers, until it runs the checker after the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over). The ground is in the language (P-26 defines the layers): Fortress is statically typed, and it chooses a coercion by the static type. Walk, in the team's implementation, has no static types. The step has three pieces, and its size is unmeasured. First, the Scala checker is turned on under walk: walk runs with Scala off, and with Scala off `StaticChecker.java` stops with "The Java version of the type checker is gone now." Second, walk learns to evaluate the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts; it has no case for them today. Third, the components that walk's programs import are cleared of the checker's errors, each before this step or before the first program that needs it (P-33 places them; F-290 counts 624 errors in the 40 components outside the twelve).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Arrays and the model program

POSITIONS.md:93
- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: whether the array factory chooses a store for each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets the `double[]` store (P-84), B is where unboxed arithmetic happens, and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). For decision A, the curator leans toward the class loader, the team's own direction, unless a clear reason appears; this is a lean to confirm, not a decision, and that way is unmeasured. The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.

(**
Access to configuration information specific to a run of a Fortress program.
Examples include command-line arguments, environment variables,
registry parameters, and the like.
**)
(** args is a top-level variable containing any command-line
    arguments.  It is an arbitrary-sized 1-D array.  Unlike C's argv,
    args does *not* include the program name.  Programmers should use
    programName to access this information.
**)
args : ImmutableArray[\String,ZZ32\] = getProgramArgs(getProgramArgsPrim())
getProgramArgsPrim(): ImmutableArray[\String,ZZ32\] = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.StringPrim$GetProgramArgs")
(* Impedence matcher to get types right.  Sigh. *)
getProgramArgs[\T extends String, int n\](r0:PrimImmutableArray[\T,n\]): PrimImmutableArray[\String,n\] =
    r0.replica[\String\]().tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32): String => r0.get(i))
(** programName is the name by which the Fortress program was invoked. **)
programName : String = ""
(** A way to get environment information from inside of fortress *)
getEnvironment(name:String, defaultValue:String):String = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.StringPrim$GetEnvironment")
(** A way to get fortress-style property information (that can be
   overridden by environment variable settings; uses the same code as
   property settings for the fortress implementation itself). *)
getProperty(name:String, defaultValue:String):String = builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.StringPrim$GetProperty")
(** Turn string into properly-terminated directory name
    (on Unix/Windows, add a trailing / if one is missing and string is nonempty) **)
toDirectoryName(s: String): String = do
    l = |s|
    if l>0 AND: s[l-1]=/='/' then s "/" else s end
  end
end

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.
